newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan parties agree to reforms amid split.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan parties agree to reforms amid split.

text.p: Taiwan's two biggest parties reached a major consensus on political reforms at a state-sponsored multiparty conference on Friday, hours after an angry opposition group announced its withdrawal from the forum.

The ruling Nationalist Party and leading opposition Democratic Progressive Party reached "significant consensus" at the National Development Conference, agreeing to freeze all elections at the provincial government level, state radio said.

"The two parties have agreed to freeze provincial governor and assembly elections in order to save state resources and increase government efficiency," Nationalist lawmaker and deputy convenor of the forum Vincent Siew said on the radio.
The jurisdictions of Taiwan's central government and the provincial government overlap considerably.
Taipei says its Republic of China government includes both the island and the Chinese mainland, though it acknowledges that the mainland is ruled by Beijing's People's Republic of China government.
"It is not intended to marginalise the provincial government but to rationalise and simplify its function," Siew said.
Opponents have argued that China, which has viewed Taiwan as a renegade province since the Chinese civil war ended in 1949, may see the move as a step closer to the island's independence.
Under the agreements, the central government would set up a special committee to reduce the redundancy of the provincial bureaucracy, Siew was quoted as saying.
The parties also agreed to freeze the National Assembly elections and expand the scale and function of the Legislative Yuan, or parliament, the radio quoted Siew as saying.

Agreements reached at the state-sponsored conference are not legally binding. But President Lee Teng-hui, who proposed the all-party conference during his May 20 inaugural address, has said he would implement the agreements as soon as possible.
The government has said it believed some common ground could be discovered during the meeting, which was intended to build consensus and sketch out a grand blueprint for Taiwan's future.
The week-long meeting concludes on Saturday.
Earlier on Friday, the fledgling New Party said it would no longer take part in the conference. It accused the Nationalist Party of manipulating the forum and of refusing to compromise.
"Our opinions did not receive proper attention and respect. We feel we have no choice but to withdraw," New Party leader Chen Kuei-miao told reporters.

The New Party disagreed sharply with the ruling party on political reforms including a proposal to abolish or marginalise Taiwan's provincial government, and said it would not endorse the Nationalists' package.
"We have tried our best to make all parties stay in the conference until the end," Nationalist Party secretary-general Wu Poh-hsiung said. "We are very sorry about the New Party's withdrawal."

On the agenda for the forum are constitutional reforms and party politics, economic development and relations between Taiwan and communist China, the island's giant neighbour and diplomatic arch rival.
Participants include senior officials, party and business leaders, investors, academics and other Taiwan elites.
